The Indian legal system is rooted in common law principles established during the British colonial era, subsequently modified, codified, and governed by the Constitution of India, 1950. Section 307 Attempt to murder Cognizable, Non-Bailable Imprisonment up to 10 years (or life if hurt is caused) and fine. Section 324 Voluntarily causing hurt by dangerous weapons Cognizable, Bailable (if compounded) Imprisonment up to 3 years, or fine, or both. Section 354 Assault or criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty Cognizable, Non-Bailable Imprisonment between 1 to 5 years and fine. Section 378 / 379 Theft (Dishonest removal of movable property) Cognizable, Bailable (Compoundable with court leave) Imprisonment up to 3 years, or fine, or both. Section 390 / 392 Robbery (Theft with immediate threat of death/hurt) Cognizable, Non-Bailable Rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years and fine. Section 406 Criminal breach of trust Cognizable, Non-Bailable Imprisonment up to 3 years, or fine, or both. Section 420 Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property Cognizable, Bailable (Compoundable in some states) Imprisonment up to 7 years and fine. Section 498A Husband or relative of husband subjecting woman to cruelty Cognizable, Non-Bailable, Non- Compoundable Imprisonment up to 3 years and fine. Section 503 / 506 Criminal intimidation (Threatening injury to person/property) Bailable (Cognizable in specific states) Imprisonment up to 2 years, or fine, or both. Section 120B Punishment of criminal conspiracy Cognizable, Non-Bailable Same as provided for the primary offence conspired. 3. Charge Sheet (Police Report) - Section 173 CrPC: Filed by the investigating agency before the jurisdictional magistrate upon completion of inquiry, detailing evidence and arraigned accused persons. Framing of Charges: The court reviews the police report and documents, hears both prosecution and defense, and formally frames charges if a prima facie case is established. Trial Proceedings: Examination-in-chief, cross-examination, and re-examination of prosecution and defense witnesses, followed by arguments. Judgment & Sentencing: Acquittal or conviction of the accused, followed by a sentencing hearing in cases of conviction. 4. CIVIL LAW: NATURE, DISPUTES, AND REMEDIES Civil law deals with disputes between private individuals, corporate entities, or institutions concerning civil rights, property, contracts, torts, and family matters. Unlike criminal cases where the state prosecutes offenders, civil cases are initiated by aggrieved plaintiffs seeking specific remedies. 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. Major Categories of Civil Cases Property and Land Disputes: Title suits, partition suits, eviction proceedings, easements, and injunctions regarding immovable property under the Specific Relief Act, 1963. Contractual Breaches: Failure to perform commercial obligations, recovery of money, specific performance of contracts, and damages for breach. Family and Matrimonial Law: Divorce, restitution of conjugal rights, child custody, maintenance, and succession under personal laws (Hindu Marriage Act, Shariat Act, Indian Succession Act, etc.). Torts and Civil Wrongs: Defamation, negligence, professional malpractice, and nuisance resulting in civil damages. 4.2. Civil Case Procedure (CPC Framework) Civil litigation is governed by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC): Presentation of Plaint (Order VII CPC): The plaintiff files a formal plaint detailing facts, cause of action, and reliefs sought. Issuance of Summons (Order V CPC): The court issues summons directing the defendant to appear and file a Written Statement.

XYZ Company retains different categories of data for different durations based on legal obligations and business necessity. Employee records are kept for 7 years after separation. Customer transaction data is retained for 5 years. Marketing analytics data is purged after 2 years. System logs and audit trails are retained for 12 months unless a legal hold is in place. All data is securely deleted via DoD 5220.22-M compliant wiping after the retention window expires. Q: Who owns the data employees create on company systems? All intellectual property, documents, code, designs, and communications created using company systems, during work hours, or as part of job duties are the exclusive property of XYZ Company. Personal data inadvertently stored on company devices must be declared to IT within 30 days for proper segregation. Q: How is personal employee data protected? Employee PII (personally identifiable information) is encrypted at rest (AES-256) and in transit (TLS 1.3). Access is role-based, with HR and Payroll holding the only elevated privileges. knowledgePreview: COMPENDIUM OF INDIAN CRIMINAL AND CIVIL LAW An Authoritative Reference Guide Detailing IPC / BNS Sections, Punishments, Criminal Trial Procedures, and Civil Litigation Frameworks in India Notice & Purpose: This legal document serves as an exhaustive reference manual outlining foundational substantive laws, procedural mechanisms, penal codes, and judicial remedies under the Indian legal framework. It covers the Indian Penal Code (IPC), Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), Code of Civil Procedure (CPC), and associated statutory punishments. 1. INTRODUCTION TO THE INDIAN LEGAL SYSTEM 1.1. The Indian legal system is rooted in common law principles established during the British colonial era, subsequently modified, codified, and governed by the Constitution of India, 1950. Indian law is broadly bifurcated into two primary branches: Substantive Law (defining rights, duties, and offenses, e.g., IPC) and Procedural Law (governing the enforcement of rights and conduct of trials, e.g., CrPC and CPC). 1.2. Hierarchy of Courts: Judicial administration follows a strict hierarchical pyramid comprising the Supreme Court of India at the apex, followed by High Courts at the state level, Sessions and District Courts at the district level, and Judicial/Civil Magistrate courts at the grassroots level. 2. CRIMINAL LAW: MAJOR IPC SECTIONS AND PUNISHMENTS Criminal jurisprudence in India defines offenses against the state, human body, property, and public tranquility. Below is a detailed tabulation of key sections under the Indian Penal Code (IPC), their descriptions, and corresponding statutory punishments: OFFICIAL LEGAL COMPENDIUM - INDIAN JURISPRUDENCE Page 1 of 3 IPC Section Offence Description Nature / Bailability Statutory Punishment Section 302 Punishment for Murder Cognizable, Non-Bailable, Non- Compoundable Death penalty or Imprisonment for Life, and fine. Section 304 Culpable homicide not amounting to murder Cognizable, Non-Bailable Imprisonment for life, or imprisonment up to 10 years and fine. Section 307 Attempt to murder Cognizable, Non-Bailable Imprisonment up to 10 years (or life if hurt is caused) and fine. Section 324 Voluntarily causing hurt by dangerous weapons Cognizable, Bailable (if compounded) Imprisonment up to 3 years, or fine, or both. Section 354 Assault or criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty Cognizable, Non-Bailable Imprisonment between 1 to 5 years and fine. Section 378 / 379 Theft (Dishonest removal of movable property) Cognizable, Bailable (Compoundable with court leave) Imprisonment up to 3 years, or fine, or both. Section 390 / 392 Robbery (Theft with immediate threat of death/hurt) Cognizable, Non-Bailable Rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years and fine. Section 406 Criminal breach of trust Cognizable, Non-Bailable Imprisonment up to 3 years, or fine, or both. Section 420 Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property Cognizable, Bailable (Compoundable in some states) Imprisonment up to 7 years and fine. Section 498A Husband or relative of husband subjecting woman to cruelty Cognizable, Non-Bailable, Non- Compoundable Imprisonment up to 3 years and fine. Section 503 / 506 Criminal intimidation (Threatening injury to person/property) Bailable (Cognizable in specific states) Imprisonment up to 2 years, or fine, or both. Section 120B Punishment of criminal conspiracy Cognizable, Non-Bailable Same as provided for the primary offence conspired. 3. CRIMINAL CASE PROCEDURE (CRPC / BNSS FRAMEWORK) The initiation, investigation, and trial of a criminal case follow a mandatory statutory procedure: First Information Report (FIR) - Section 154 CrPC: Recorded by a police officer upon receiving information regarding the commission of a cognizable offence. Police Investigation - Chapter XII CrPC: Collection of evidence, examination of witnesses, inspection of crime scenes, and arrest of suspects where necessary. Charge Sheet (Police Report) - Section 173 CrPC: Filed by the investigating agency before the jurisdictional magistrate upon completion of inquiry, detailing evidence and arraigned accused persons. Framing of Charges: The court reviews the police report and documents, hears both prosecution and defense, and formally frames charges if a prima facie case is established. Trial Proceedings: Examination-in-chief, cross-examination, and re-examination of prosecution and defense witnesses, followed by arguments. Judgment & Sentencing: Acquittal or conviction of the accused, followed by a sentencing hearing in cases of conviction. 4. CIVIL LAW: NATURE, DISPUTES, AND REMEDIES Civil law deals with disputes between private individuals, corporate entities, or institutions concerning civil rights, property, contracts, torts, and family matters. Unlike criminal cases where the state prosecutes offenders, civil cases are initiated by aggrieved plaintiffs seeking specific remedies. 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. OFFICIAL LEGAL COMPENDIUM - INDIAN JURISPRUDENCE Page 2 of 3 4.1. Major Categories of Civil Cases Property and Land Disputes: Title suits, partition suits, eviction proceedings, easements, and injunctions regarding immovable property under the Specific Relief Act, 1963. Contractual Breaches: Failure to perform commercial obligations, recovery of money, specific performance of contracts, and damages for breach. Family and Matrimonial Law: Divorce, restitution of conjugal rights, child custody, maintenance, and succession under personal laws (Hindu Marriage Act, Shariat Act, Indian Succession Act, etc.). Torts and Civil Wrongs: Defamation, negligence, professional malpractice, and nuisance resulting in civil damages. 4.2. Civil Case Procedure (CPC Framework) Civil litigation is governed by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC): Presentation of Plaint (Order VII CPC): The plaintiff files a formal plaint detailing facts, cause of action, and reliefs sought. Issuance of Summons (Order V CPC): The court issues summons directing the defendant to appear and file a Written Statement.

It covers the Indian Penal Code (IPC), Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), Code of Civil Procedure (CPC), and associated statutory punishments. 1. INTRODUCTION TO THE INDIAN LEGAL SYSTEM 1.1. The Indian legal system is rooted in common law principles established during the British colonial era, subsequently modified, codified, and governed by the Constitution of India, 1950. Indian law is broadly bifurcated into two primary branches: Substantive Law (defining rights, duties, and offenses, e.g., IPC) and Procedural Law (governing the enforcement of rights and conduct of trials, e.g., CrPC and CPC). 1.2. Hierarchy of Courts: Judicial administration follows a strict hierarchical pyramid comprising the Supreme Court of India at the apex, followed by High Courts at the state level, Sessions and District Courts at the district level, and Judicial/Civil Magistrate courts at the grassroots level. 2. CRIMINAL LAW: MAJOR IPC SECTIONS AND PUNISHMENTS Criminal jurisprudence in India defines offenses against the state, human body, property, and public tranquility. Below is a detailed tabulation of key sections under the Indian Penal Code (IPC), their descriptions, and corresponding statutory punishments: OFFICIAL LEGAL COMPENDIUM - INDIAN JURISPRUDENCE Page 1 of 3 IPC Section Offence Description Nature / Bailability Statutory Punishment Section 302 Punishment for Murder Cognizable, Non-Bailable, Non- Compoundable Death penalty or Imprisonment for Life, and fine. Section 304 Culpable homicide not amounting to murder Cognizable, Non-Bailable Imprisonment for life, or imprisonment up to 10 years and fine. Section 307 Attempt to murder Cognizable, Non-Bailable Imprisonment up to 10 years (or life if hurt is caused) and fine. Section 324 Voluntarily causing hurt by dangerous weapons Cognizable, Bailable (if compounded) Imprisonment up to 3 years, or fine, or both. Section 354 Assault or criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty Cognizable, Non-Bailable Imprisonment between 1 to 5 years and fine. Section 378 / 379 Theft (Dishonest removal of movable property) Cognizable, Bailable (Compoundable with court leave) Imprisonment up to 3 years, or fine, or both. Section 390 / 392 Robbery (Theft with immediate threat of death/hurt) Cognizable, Non-Bailable Rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years and fine. Section 406 Criminal breach of trust Cognizable, Non-Bailable Imprisonment up to 3 years, or fine, or both. Section 420 Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property Cognizable, Bailable (Compoundable in some states) Imprisonment up to 7 years and fine. Section 498A Husband or relative of husband subjecting woman to cruelty Cognizable, Non-Bailable, Non- Compoundable Imprisonment up to 3 years and fine. Section 503 / 506 Criminal intimidation (Threatening injury to person/property) Bailable (Cognizable in specific states) Imprisonment up to 2 years, or fine, or both. Section 120B Punishment of criminal conspiracy Cognizable, Non-Bailable Same as provided for the primary offence conspired. 3. CRIMINAL CASE PROCEDURE (CRPC / BNSS FRAMEWORK) The initiation, investigation, and trial of a criminal case follow a mandatory statutory procedure: First Information Report (FIR) - Section 154 CrPC: Recorded by a police officer upon receiving information regarding the commission of a cognizable offence. Police Investigation - Chapter XII CrPC: Collection of evidence, examination of witnesses, inspection of crime scenes, and arrest of suspects where necessary. Charge Sheet (Police Report) - Section 173 CrPC: Filed by the investigating agency before the jurisdictional magistrate upon completion of inquiry, detailing evidence and arraigned accused persons. Framing of Charges: The court reviews the police report and documents, hears both prosecution and defense, and formally frames charges if a prima facie case is established. Trial Proceedings: Examination-in-chief, cross-examination, and re-examination of prosecution and defense witnesses, followed by arguments. Judgment & Sentencing: Acquittal or conviction of the accused, followed by a sentencing hearing in cases of conviction. 4. CIVIL LAW: NATURE, DISPUTES, AND REMEDIES Civil law deals with disputes between private individuals, corporate entities, or institutions concerning civil rights, property, contracts, torts, and family matters. Unlike criminal cases where the state prosecutes offenders, civil cases are initiated by aggrieved plaintiffs seeking specific remedies. 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. OFFICIAL LEGAL COMPENDIUM - INDIAN JURISPRUDENCE Page 2 of 3 4.1. Major Categories of Civil Cases Property and Land Disputes: Title suits, partition suits, eviction proceedings, easements, and injunctions regarding immovable property under the Specific Relief Act, 1963. Contractual Breaches: Failure to perform commercial obligations, recovery of money, specific performance of contracts, and damages for breach. Family and Matrimonial Law: Divorce, restitution of conjugal rights, child custody, maintenance, and succession under personal laws (Hindu Marriage Act, Shariat Act, Indian Succession Act, etc.). Torts and Civil Wrongs: Defamation, negligence, professional malpractice, and nuisance resulting in civil damages. 4.2. Civil Case Procedure (CPC Framework) Civil litigation is governed by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC): Presentation of Plaint (Order VII CPC): The plaintiff files a formal plaint detailing facts, cause of action, and reliefs sought. Issuance of Summons (Order V CPC): The court issues summons directing the defendant to appear and file a Written Statement.
